A column by Dr. Tony Leachon offers what he calls a dramatic “wake up call” about the health of Filipinos. At first glance, the argument sounds persuasive. It cites life expectancy statistics and appeals to urgency and moral responsibility. But a closer look shows the narrative quickly weakens. The piece relies on selective comparisons, ignores structural realities, and reduces a complicated public health issue into a convenient political talking point.

Leachon compares Philippine life expectancy with several ASEAN countries, yet the comparison itself is misleading because it ignores major differences in wealth and development. Placing the Philippines alongside Singapore is not a meaningful benchmark. Singapore is a wealthy city state with one of the highest per capita incomes in the world, so superior health outcomes are hardly surprising. The same dynamic applies to Malaysia and Thailand, both of which benefit from higher income levels and stronger health infrastructure. Without acknowledging these economic realities, the comparison becomes rhetorical rather than analytical.

The column also overlooks the significant reforms already introduced in the Philippine health system. The Universal Health Care Act (Philippines) automatically enrolled Filipinos into the national health insurance system and greatly expanded coverage. Access to hospitalization, dialysis, and treatment for catastrophic illnesses has widened as a result. To suggest that the system simply abandons the poor ignores the millions who now receive benefits that were unavailable a decade ago.

Leachon further narrows the discussion by pointing to bureaucracy as the main reason for life expectancy gaps. In reality, health outcomes are shaped by far more than hospital funding or administrative efficiency. Road accidents, smoking, diet, urban congestion, and environmental exposure all influence mortality rates. The Philippines is also among the most disaster prone countries in the world, regularly struck by powerful typhoons that damage infrastructure and cost lives. These realities affect national health indicators in ways that cannot be reduced to bureaucratic delay.

The column also contains an internal contradiction. It criticizes government systems for allegedly failing the poor, yet it simultaneously shifts the burden to individuals by urging Filipinos to exercise more and adopt healthier lifestyles. Both ideas may hold some truth, but presenting them together as the central explanation weakens the argument. If government inefficiency is the primary problem, then lifestyle lectures are beside the point. If personal habits are the dominant factor, blaming bureaucracy alone is incomplete.

What the column ignores most is the long term progress already achieved. In the 1960s, the average Filipino lived only into the mid fifties. Today life expectancy is roughly seventy years. That improvement reflects decades of vaccination campaigns, advances in maternal care, wider access to hospitals, and gradual economic development. Portraying the present situation as a national failure erases this steady trajectory of progress.

Public health deserves analysis grounded in context and evidence. Differences in life expectancy across Southeast Asia cannot be explained by a single government program or bureaucratic delay. They are shaped by deeper forces such as economic development, demographics, geography, and institutional capacity.

In the end, the real wake up call is not the alarm raised by Tony Leachon. The real wake up call is for Filipinos to be cautious about alarmist narratives that simplify complex national challenges. Progress will come from sustained economic growth, smarter health investments, stronger institutions, and citizens who take responsibility for their own health rather than relying on dramatic rhetoric disguised as analysis.
